```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

This vignette applies the framework of Toussaint et al. (2026, *Ecography*,
doi:10.1002/ecog.08578) to the example data of the package: 2000 bird species
drawn at random from the species of that study and described by the same
traits — locomotion (five continuous traits, AVONET; Tobias et al. 2022),
reproduction (eight continuous traits, Amniote database; Myhrvold et al.
2015) and diet (ten diet categories coded as one fuzzy trait, EltonTraits;
Wilman et al. 2014). See `?birds_traits` for sources, licences and sampling.
The framework (i) groups traits into functional dimensions, (ii) builds one
functional space per dimension and one combined space, and (iii) quantifies
how congruent these spaces are, at the level of the whole space (Procrustes
tests) and of species (FUn, FSp, FUSE).

```{r}
library(DisentFunSpaces)
data(birds_traits)
dim(birds_traits)
head(birds_traits[, c("species", "family", "body_mass", "clutch_size", "diet_inv", "iucn")])
```

## 1. Describe the traits

Each trait column receives a **type** and a functional **dimension**. Columns of a
fuzzy-coded (`F`) or multichoice (`B`) trait share a **block** name.

```{r}
trait_types()[, c("code", "label")]
```

`guess_trait_info()` proposes a first draft, which must be checked: dimensions,
ordinal levels and circular limits cannot be inferred. Taxonomy and the IUCN
category are not traits and are left out; the phylogenetic eigenvectors
(`Eigen.1`-`Eigen.10`) are recognised as imputation predictors (`use = FALSE`).

```{r}
not_traits <- c("order", "family", "iucn")
draft <- guess_trait_info(birds_traits[, !names(birds_traits) %in% not_traits],
                          species_col = "species")
draft[draft$trait %in% c("body_mass", "clutch_size", "diet_inv", "diet_fruit", "Eigen.1"), 1:5]
```

The completed table assigns traits to the three dimensions of the published
analysis. The beak traits, used in the paper only to build a validation
space, are listed with `use = FALSE`:

```{r}
data(birds_trait_info)
birds_trait_info[, c("trait", "type", "dimension", "block", "transform", "use")]
```

## 2. Prepare traits and impute missing values

```{r}
traits <- prepare_traits(birds_traits, birds_trait_info, species_col = "species")
traits
```

Reproduction traits have many missing values (9 % for adult body mass, up to
85 % for body length); only `r sum(stats::complete.cases(traits$data))`
species are complete. As in the published analysis, missing values are
imputed with missForest using the first ten phylogenetic eigenvectors as
predictors (eigenvectors can also be computed from `birds_tree` with
`phylo = birds_tree`). Missing values could also be kept (the generalised
Gower distance then uses, for each pair of species, the traits available for
both) or removed with `drop_incomplete()`.

```{r}
preds <- birds_traits[, paste0("Eigen.", 1:10)]
rownames(preds) <- birds_traits$species
if (requireNamespace("missForest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  traits <- impute_traits(traits, covariates = preds, ntree = 50, seed = 1)
  print(traits$imputation$oob)
} else {
  traits <- drop_incomplete(traits)   # fallback when missForest is not installed
}
length(traits$species)
```

## 3. Build the functional spaces

`build_space()` assembles the traits of the selected dimensions into one
table per dimension × type (fuzzy and multichoice traits prepared with
`ade4::prep.fuzzy()` / `ade4::prep.binary()`) and calls `PCoAGraph()`, the
core function of the published analysis: `ade4::ktab.list.df()` →
`ade4::dist.ktab(option = "scaledBYrange")` → `ape::pcoa()` →
`vegan::envfit()` and `CorrelType()`. By default one space per dimension plus
a `Combined` space. `engine = "fast"` gives the same distances as
`ade4::dist.ktab()` (vectorised; see `?trait_distance`) and is faster for
thousands of species:

```{r}
spaces <- build_spaces(traits, envfit_perm = 0, engine = "fast")
spaces
spaces$Combined$blocks$groups   # types of the tables passed to dist.ktab
```

As in the published analysis, the first axis of the combined space is a size
gradient (body mass, wing length, egg mass), whereas diet only structures the
second axis:

```{r}
round(spaces$Combined$PCoACor[, 1:2], 2)
```

```{r}
plot_space(spaces$Combined)
plot_space(spaces$Diet)
plot_quality(lapply(spaces, space_quality, max_axes = 8))
```

## 4. Compare spaces with Procrustes tests

```{r}
cmp <- compare_spaces(spaces, nrepet = 199)
cmp
plot_comparison(cmp)
```

Locomotion and reproduction spaces are strongly congruent (both largely
driven by body size), whereas the diet space is only weakly congruent with
them.

`weighting = "variable"` (default) reproduces the published analysis: a
single `ade4::dist.ktab()` call in which each continuous trait and the
fuzzy-coded diet block count as one variable each, so that the combined
squared distance is (5 d²~Locomotion~ + 8 d²~Reproduction~ + 1 d²~Diet~) / 14.
Two dimension-level weightings are available. With `"dimension"` each
dimension has the same weight; because Manly distances between diet profiles
are on average much larger than range-scaled distances between continuous
traits, diet then dominates the combined space. `"dimension_scaled"` divides
the squared distances of each dimension by their mean before averaging, so
that each dimension contributes equally on average:

```{r}
dims <- c("Locomotion", "Reproduction", "Diet")
for (w in c("dimension", "dimension_scaled")) {
  spaces[[w]] <- build_space(traits, dims, name = w, weighting = w,
                             envfit_perm = 0, engine = "fast")
}
r_comb <- function(nm) {
  tb <- compare_spaces(spaces[c(dims, nm)], nrepet = 99)$table
  setNames(tb$r[tb$space2 == nm], tb$space1[tb$space2 == nm])
}
round(rbind(variable = r_comb("Combined"), dimension = r_comb("dimension"),
            dimension_scaled = r_comb("dimension_scaled")), 2)
spaces$dimension <- spaces$dimension_scaled <- NULL
```

The robustness of the conclusions to the number of axes can be explored with
`n_axes` (e.g. `compare_spaces(spaces, n_axes = 2)`, as the first two axes
were retained in the published analysis).

Species whose functional position differs most between two spaces:

```{r}
res <- procrustes_residuals(spaces$Diet, spaces$Combined)
head(res)
plot_procrustes(res)
```

### Validation space: beak morphology

The published analysis excluded beak traits from the locomotion space and
used them to build an independent validation space. Setting `use = TRUE`
for these traits adds a `Beak` dimension:

```{r}
ti_beak <- birds_trait_info
ti_beak$use <- TRUE
tr_beak <- prepare_traits(birds_traits, ti_beak, species_col = "species")
beak <- build_space(tr_beak, "Beak", envfit_perm = 0, engine = "fast")
sp_beak <- structure(list(Locomotion = spaces$Locomotion, Diet = spaces$Diet, Beak = beak),
                     class = "fs_spaces")
compare_spaces(sp_beak, nrepet = 99)
```

## 5. Species-level metrics

FUSE combines FUn and FSp with the extinction probability associated with
the IUCN category of each species (Gumbs et al. 2023):

```{r}
iucn <- setNames(birds_traits$iucn, birds_traits$species)
m <- species_metrics_all(spaces, k = 5, iucn = iucn)
head(m)
```

The species with the highest FUSE, and the sets of the most unique species,
differ between functional dimensions:

```{r}
top <- lapply(split(m, m$space), function(x) head(x$species[order(-x$FUSE)], 5))
as.data.frame(top, check.names = FALSE)
compare_metrics(m, "FUn", top = 0.1)$pairs
```

## 6. Non-native species

The bird data have no native/non-native status, so introductions are
simulated here (15% of species, biased towards the periphery of the combined
space). With real data, `status` is a named vector (`"native"` vs any other
label, e.g. `"introduced"`), or a sites x species matrix with `comm` when a
species is native in some assemblages and non-native in others.

```{r}
status <- simulate_introductions(spaces$Combined, prop = 0.15,
                                 bias = "peripheral", seed = 1)
nn <- nonnative_all(spaces, status, n_axes = 4, hull_axes = 3,
                    null = "permute", nrep = 19, seed = 1)   # use >= 999 in practice
summary_nonnative(nn)
```

`p_outside_hull` is the proportion of non-native species that expand the
native space, `FNov_rel` their mean distance to the nearest native relative
to the mean nearest-neighbour distance among natives (> 1: non-native species
are further from natives than natives are from each other), `dFUn_native_median` the
median loss of uniqueness of native species, and `ses_FRic_median` the
standardised effect of introductions on functional richness compared with
the same number of random species. Non-native species that are novel in one
dimension are not necessarily novel in another:

```{r}
compare_nonnative(nn, "FNov", top = 0.2)$pairs
plot_nonnative(spaces$Combined, status, label = 5)
```

## Shiny application

The same workflow is available interactively with `run_app()`, which also
exports the trait-information table, the results and an R script reproducing
the analysis.
